# The Repairability and Market Position of Framework Laptops

Framework brands itself around fixing "broken" consumer electronics through inherent customization and repairability [1]. The company's design philosophy trusts customers and repair shops with the access and information needed to maintain devices [1]. 

## Modular Design Philosophy and History

Framework is a San Francisco-based company known for modular and upgradable laptops [1]. Its core philosophy relies on well-considered design tradeoffs to make devices easy to repair [1]. The company recently paused US sales of certain base systems in its Laptop 13 series due to a 32% reciprocal tariff on Taiwan, stating that selling them at current prices would result in a loss [1]. 

## Repairability and Upgradeability vs. Traditional Laptop Brands

When purchasing a Framework Laptop, users buy a mainboard along with a keyboard, touchpad, RAM, SSD, and ports that can be self-assembled in about 20 minutes using a single screwdriver [5]. Components are well-organized and labeled, offering the potential for an heirloom device that remains repairable and upgradable for a decade [6]. While the repair aspect is well-developed, the upfront price is higher than equivalent models from mainstream brands [4][5]. Framework remains a niche startup for enthusiasts, holding a tiny market presence compared to major manufacturers like Apple, Dell, HP, Lenovo, and Asus [5]. Furthermore, some users note that other manufacturers offer similar modularity at half the price using standard components, and certain Framework desktop motherboards use soldered RAM [4]. 

## Criticisms and Limitations Regarding Cost and Performance

Framework laptops face several primary criticisms, notably their high cost (such as a $1,400 price tag for a configuration compared to a $900 laptop) and expensive expansion cards [7]. Critics also point out that parts are effectively proprietary because no other companies manufacture parts for Framework laptops [7]. Hardware reviews note specific drawbacks: the Framework 16 has been described as a mediocre machine with a mediocre display, heat and fan noise issues, poor battery life, and subpar performance [8]. Additionally, component prices can be so high that users might be better off selling an old unit and buying a new laptop entirely, undermining the upgrade purpose [8]. The company has been transparent about component struggles and steady price increases [9].

NO SOURCES FOUND

## Conclusion

Framework has successfully demonstrated that modular, user-serviceable laptops can function in the consumer market, appealing directly to repair enthusiasts [5]. However, high upfront and component costs, proprietary part limitations, and performance drawbacks continue to restrict its appeal primarily to niche markets rather than mainstream consumers [5][7][8].
